A1-A2.headline: How Antibiotics Are Used On Farms Today

pages.text: Farmers use medicine to keep animals healthy. About 73% of all medicine is used for farm animals. This is a big number. Experts worry this can cause germs that do not die. This means medicine might not work well for us in the future.
pages.caption: Germs move from farm animals to humans.

evidence.articleCaption: A CDC infographic on how antibiotic-resistant bacteria have the potential to spread from farm animals

pages.text: In the past, farmers used medicine to help animals grow fast. This is now changing. The European Union stopped this in 2006. The United States also made new laws in 2017. These laws stop using important medicine just to make animals grow bigger and faster.

The World Health Organization says we must use less medicine in food. They worry about the risk of germs that do not die. Some countries still use a lot of medicine. This is often because they have crowded farms. Experts say this is a serious risk for our health.

Farmers must follow safety rules. They wait before selling meat or milk. This time helps the medicine leave the animal's body. Scientists also look for new ways to keep animals healthy, like using good food choices. These are healthy for animals.

B1-B2.headline: Managing Antibiotic Use Within Global Livestock Production Systems

pages.text: Drugs are vital for treating animal disease and ensuring food safety. However, global use is high, with farm animals accounting for 73% of total use. This widespread application raises concerns about drug resistance, which threatens human and animal health by reducing the effectiveness of essential medical treatments.
pages.caption: Drug resistance can spread from animals to humans.

evidence.articleCaption: A CDC infographic on how antibiotic-resistant bacteria have the potential to spread from farm animals

pages.text: In the past, drugs were used to help animals grow and improve feed efficiency. Many regions have now set stricter rules. The European Union banned growth drugs in 2006. The United States followed in 2017 by banning important drugs for growth purposes.

In 2017, the World Health Organization recommended reducing drug use in food animals to stop the threat of resistance. Despite this, money often drives high use in crowded conditions. Experts warn that without change, we face a future where common diseases become hard to treat.

To protect people, rules require waiting periods before animal products enter the food supply. This ensures that any given medicine has left the animal's system. Researchers are also exploring alternatives that support animal health, offering a path toward better farming practices.

C1-C2.headline: Navigating the Complexities of Antimicrobial Stewardship in Global Agriculture

pages.text: Antibiotics serve as a cornerstone of modern veterinary medicine, yet their pervasive use in livestock production poses significant public health challenges. With approximately 73% of global antimicrobials utilized in agriculture, the potential for the emergence of resistant bacteria is profound. This trend threatens to undermine the efficacy of medical interventions, necessitating a critical re-evaluation of current husbandry practices.
pages.caption: Resistant bacteria migrate from livestock to humans.

evidence.articleCaption: A CDC infographic on how antibiotic-resistant bacteria have the potential to spread from farm animals

pages.text: Historically, the agricultural sector leveraged sub-therapeutic antibiotic doses to enhance feed conversion and accelerate growth. However, this paradigm has shifted due to mounting evidence of environmental and health risks. Regulatory bodies, including the European Union and the FDA, have enacted stringent prohibitions on the use of medically important antibiotics for growth promotion to mitigate the proliferation of resistance.

The World Health Organization’s 2017 recommendations underscore the urgency of curbing antibiotic reliance in the food industry. Despite these directives, economic pressures in intensive farming environments frequently incentivize continued high usage. Addressing these systemic issues is imperative, as the unchecked development of antimicrobial resistance could fundamentally compromise the future of both human and veterinary medical efficacy.

Rigorous adherence to drug withdrawal periods remains a fundamental safety protocol, ensuring that animal-derived products are free from chemical residues. Beyond regulatory compliance, the industry is increasingly investigating innovative alternatives, such as prebiotics, to optimize animal health. These advancements represent a pivotal move toward reconciling agricultural productivity with the broader imperatives of global health and environmental sustainability.
